summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel SOSCF v. Lucas
key_cases.holding: The court held good cause existed to deny the tribe's transfer motion filed after most of the termination trial had been completed, and addressed the qualified expert witness requirement under ICWA.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Oregon authority on good cause to deny a tribe's mid-trial motion to transfer an Indian child's case to tribal court, and on the qualified-expert-witness requirement.
key_cases.quote: We hold that good cause existed to deny the motion to transfer jurisdiction to the tribe.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. J. G.
key_cases.holding: The court held that ICWA § 1914 permits an unpreserved 'active efforts' claim to be raised for the first time on appeal, but that ICWA did not require an active-efforts finding in a durable guardianship judgment, and affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Explains when ICWA's active-efforts requirement attaches to a particular Oregon juvenile proceeding and why the ordinary preservation rule yields to § 1914.
key_cases.quote: the juvenile court was not required under ICWA to make an "active efforts" finding in the guardianship judgment

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's Article I authority to enact it and rejecting the anticommandeering attacks on its placement and record-keeping provisions, while holding that no petitioner had standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation claims.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that ICWA's placement preferences and related commands are constitutional and binding on Oregon juvenile courts, which is the unstated premise of every ORICWA application in this brief.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. A. N.
key_cases.holding: On de novo review in an ICWA case, the court held mother was unfit but that the State failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination was in the child's best interest where he was placed long-term with bonded extended family, and reversed.
key_cases.relevance: Illustrates how ICWA's heightened burden of proof applies to every fact supporting termination once the tribe gives notice of membership.
key_cases.quote: DHS has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination of mother's parental rights is in his best interest

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. R. F.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of former foster parents' ORS 419B.116 motion to intervene in an ICWA case, holding the juvenile court was not compelled to find that existing parties could not adequately present the placement question, while noting intervention might later be required.
key_cases.relevance: Applies ORICWA and ICWA placement-preference machinery, including the tribe's authority to say who counts as a relative placement.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, the Fs have not demonstrated that the juvenile court committed reversible error when it denied the motion to intervene.

reporting_details: Oregon is not a universal-reporting state: only the “public or private officials” listed in Or. Rev. Stat. § 419B.005(6) must immediately report suspected child abuse, and they report through the centralized Oregon Child Abuse Hotline or to a local law enforcement agency (Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 419B.010(1), 419B.015(1)(a)); the duty is personal to the official regardless of any employer’s internal reporting policy (§ 419B.010(3), (4)), privileged communications to a psychiatrist, psychologist, member of the clergy, attorney or guardian ad litem are excepted (§ 419B.010(1)), failure to report is a Class A violation (§ 419B.010(5)), and any other person may report voluntarily (§ 419B.015(1)(a)).
